records.name: Single-cell & spatial profiling
records.tldr: Bulk, cell or nucleus profiling, and spatial RNA methods attach measurements to different units and retain different context.
records.summary: Bulk RNA pools a specimen; cell or nucleus profiling separates recovered profiles; spatial methods retain capture positions or decoded molecule coordinates. Spots can contain several cells, and segmentation or imputation adds inference. Split aliquots and adjacent sections are not the same cells. Recovery, measured genes, physical resolution, replication and intended use determine which question each method can address.

notes: Bulk RNA reports pooled abundance, cell or nucleus profiling reports recovered profiles, and spatial measurement attaches observations to tissue positions. A capture position can contain multiple cells. Directly observed RNA, cell assignments and model-imputed expression are distinct outputs. The original positional capture study examined mouse brain and human breast cancer tissue. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/27365449/.

Fictional comparison exercise: 60 immune-assigned profiles among 300 recovered nuclei is 20% of recovered profiles. It does not establish 20% tissue area or original cell abundance. Split aliquots and adjacent sections are not the same cells. Biological replication and recovery bias still constrain cross-method comparisons. Source for biological-replicate requirements: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34584091/.
The axis that differs is the measured unit and the context still attached: pooled specimen, recovered cell or nucleus profile, or capture position or decoded molecule coordinates.
Estimating cell sources from a bulk mixture needs assumptions and references and is not direct counting.

Single-cell uses barcodes; whole cells capture nuclear and cytoplasmic RNA while nuclei mainly nuclear RNA; dissociation and filtering affect recovery; profile-based identity is an assignment, not proof of malignancy.

A spatial capture spot or bin can contain several cells; imaging locates decoded molecules but segmentation affects cell-level reading; observed molecule, assigned cell and imputed value are different outputs.
Adjacent sections or split aliquots are not the same cells; two libraries from one portion are technical repeats of one biological specimen.
Cells from one specimen are not independent biological replicates.
Fictional teaching exercise: Of 300 recovered nuclei, 60 immune is 20% of recovered nuclei, not a tissue-area or original-cell fraction.

Budget finite tissue, aliquots and sections for each compatible preparation. Report counts or normalised abundance per pool, recovered cell/nucleus or spatial unit, with physical resolution, measured genes and cell-boundary rules. Quality criteria, recovery, processing/imaging/analysis cost and controls vary by assay. Independent specimens support biological comparisons; attractive maps and technical repeats do not provide clinical validation.

OnCo reading inference: finer spatial resolution does not automatically provide broader measured-gene coverage or more complete recovery. A missing RNA count can reflect preparation or detection limits; an inferred cell source or protein activity is a different kind of output.

Two independent choices shape a spatial assay: which molecule is measured, and which area is sampled. Antibody-based imaging detects selected proteins through fluorescent or metal tags; RNA probes and barcoded capture detect selected transcripts or captured RNA. A protein-targeting question needs evidence about the protein on the relevant cells. Transcription alone does not establish protein abundance or cell-surface localisation. These maps describe the sampled preparation, rather than every part of a tumour.

Choose the molecular layer and sampling design together. Broad RNA measurement can support discovery of genes, cell states and pathways before selecting a smaller marker panel. Regional digital spatial profiling compares compartments selected by an operator and can measure protein or RNA, but a pooled regional count does not identify which individual cells carry the signal. Imaging across a complete chosen field can reveal borders, neighbourhoods and rare cells outside a predefined compartment; the imaged field still need not cover the whole slide. Report who selected the regions and by what rule.

Cell-level interpretation requires justified cell boundaries and cell-type calls. It is not a prerequisite for every spatial output: pooled regions and capture spots can be analysed without assigning every signal to a cell. Tissue-section examples also do not define every possible spatial experiment. Chen and colleagues demonstrated MERFISH imaging of 100 to 1,000 selected RNA species as individual molecules in cultured human fibroblasts. Molecule localisation and assignment to cells remain distinct steps. Validate each antibody or probe, registration and relevant cell assignments for the actual preparation; spatial resolution and gene or protein coverage remain separate properties.

In a fictional comparison, a 40-marker panel lacking the relevant target cannot answer the target question that a suitable six-marker panel can address. With one spare tissue section and a question about target-bearing cancer cells near T cells, use validated protein detection for the target, cancer cells and T cells over a justified area, with appropriate controls and cell assignments. Regional RNA alone would not establish which cells carry that protein. Budget the finite section before choosing the assay; changing the question after tissue is used does not recover the material.

A multiplex research panel and a validated clinical receptor or PD-L1 immunohistochemistry assay have different evidence requirements. Marker count, a detailed image and a reproducible measurement do not confer treatment-selection validity. Check the exact assay, scoring rule, population and intended use rather than transferring the status of a clinical single-marker assay to a different research panel.
records.principle: RNA is captured with barcodes per cell or per spatial location, or read by imaging-based in situ hybridisation for hundreds to thousands of genes.
strengths: Retains spatial context in compatible workflows
limitations: Preparation, recovery and analysis affect results
Clinical utility requires evidence for the intended use

records.name: Imaging mass cytometry
records.tldr: A way to stain a tumour slice for dozens of proteins at once using metal-tagged antibodies read by a mass spectrometer, giving a detailed map of which cells are where.
records.summary: Imaging mass cytometry (Standard BioTools Hyperion) and multiplexed ion beam imaging (MIBI) label antibodies with rare-earth metal isotopes instead of fluorophores, then ablate the tissue pixel by pixel and read the metals by mass spectrometry. Forty or more markers can be measured on one section without spectral overlap, letting researchers phenotype immune and tumour cells in place and quantify their spatial relationships.

notes: Historical method examples establish what was measured in those experiments. Giesen and colleagues reported simultaneous imaging of 32 proteins and protein modifications at subcellular resolution in human breast-cancer samples in 2014, using metal-tagged antibodies and high-resolution laser ablation coupled to mass cytometry. Ablation consumes the sampled area. The 32-marker example is not a present instrument ceiling, and Lin and colleagues' 2018 t-CyCIF study used conventional optical microscopes for up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded specimens. Each example retains its method, molecular layer and preparation.

Keren and colleagues used multiplexed ion-beam imaging to measure 36 proteins in 41 triple-negative breast-cancer patients in 2018. Their image processing included cell segmentation, and spatial analysis distinguished immune-mixed from compartmentalised tumours. Organised border structures and compartmentalisation were linked to survival in this cohort. These observations neither establish that adjacent cells are functionally interacting nor constitute a trial selecting treatment by the pattern.
records.principle: Metal-isotope-tagged antibodies bind the section; a laser or ion beam vaporises each pixel and time-of-flight mass spectrometry counts the isotopes, building one image per marker.
limitations: Slow acquisition and small fields of view

records.name: Multiplex immunofluorescence
records.tldr: This approach measures several protein markers in a tissue section, in one or more imaging cycles. Image analysis then estimates cells, counts and distances under defined rules.
records.summary: Multiplex immunofluorescence measures selected protein-marker signals in a tissue section, using one or several imaging cycles. Cyclic methods build a high-plex image of one section by repeating staining, imaging and signal removal and then registering the cycles: t-CyCIF produced up to 60-plex images of formalin-fixed specimens and showed that antigenicity changes with cycle number (Lin and colleagues, 2018), and IBEX imaged more than 65 parameters in one section by iterative staining and chemical bleaching (Radtke and colleagues, 2020). A six-institution study of a six-plex PD-1 and PD-L1 panel, imaged with a locked-down image analysis algorithm, reported average intersite concordance of cell densities of R squared 0.75 in breast carcinoma and 0.72 in non-small cell lung cancer tissue microarrays (Taube and colleagues, 2021); that is reproducibility for one specified panel and workflow, not for multiplex immunofluorescence in general. A cell phenotype is a rule-based call from the measured panel, a density needs a stated denominator, and a distance needs a stated definition (cell centre or cell boundary).

notes: Assay card for multiplex immunofluorescence (a reading guide, not a score). Input and tissue cost: a compatible fixed or frozen section; staining uses material and may involve repeated processing, and the section does not preserve viable cells for a killing assay. Output and units: marker images, fluorescence intensity in assay-dependent units, cell counts, cells per square millimetre, cell fractions and defined distances in micrometres. Controls: marker-positive and marker-negative material, comparison with validated single-marker staining, channel or spectral controls, background assessment, cycle alignment and boundary overlays. Thresholds: panel-specific marker and phenotype rules locked before the intended comparison and tested for reproducibility. Failure modes: autofluorescence, overlapping signals, nonspecific antibodies, staining-order effects, tissue loss, alignment errors and incorrect cell boundaries. Cannot establish: all proteins, live-cell behaviour, antigen specificity, actual killing or universal treatment eligibility. Validation: specific to the panel, staining, imaging, analysis and intended use.

Figure reading (fictional, no cutoff): channels A and B are measured, registered marker images; the overlay adds estimated cell masks. Centre-to-centre distance includes the cell interiors, while boundary-to-boundary distance spans only the gap, so the two rulers give different numbers for the same pair. Proximity under either rule is not contact, recognition or killing.

records.name: Spatial transcriptomics
records.tldr: These methods measure RNA signals while keeping information about position in a tissue section. A measured spot, an estimated cell boundary and an imputed value are different kinds of evidence.
records.summary: Spatial transcriptomics measures RNA signals while retaining information about where they came from in a tissue section. Sequencing capture and imaging-based detection use different measurement units. A third approach, region-of-interest profiling such as digital spatial profiling, releases oligonucleotide tags only from regions an operator chooses; the method paper describes regions covering 1 to about 5,000 cells and panels of up to 44 proteins, or 1,412 genes with sequencing readout, on formalin-fixed tissue (Merritt and colleagues, 2020), so the result depends on how the regions were selected. The original sequencing-based method placed sections on arrays of positionally barcoded primers and kept two-dimensional position (Ståhl and colleagues, 2016); a capture spot is a positional barcode and can span several cells. MERFISH imaged 100 to 1,000 RNA species chosen by probe design (Chen and colleagues, 2015), a targeted gene set and not every transcript. Assigning molecules to cells depends on estimated cell boundaries: many methods approximate cell positions from nuclear stains, and distinguishing the boundaries of individual cells is challenging and can hamper downstream analysis; Baysor was developed to optimise boundaries from transcript composition and cell morphology (Petukhov and colleagues, 2022). Gene values imputed by aligning single-cell data to a spatial map, as Tangram does (shown in mouse brain; Biancalani and colleagues, 2021), are model outputs and not extra RNA molecules detected by the spatial assay.

notes: Assay card for spatial transcriptomics (a reading guide, not a score). Measures and how: RNA with coordinates, by preparing a section, capturing or probing RNA, sequencing or imaging, decoding, registering positions and reporting the assignment rules. Input and tissue cost: protocol-compatible frozen or fixed sections; sectioning and molecular preparation consume allocated material, some workflows alter or destroy the assayed section, and re-scoring existing data consumes no new tissue. Output and units: gene counts per spot, bin or assigned cell, and decoded molecule coordinates, often in micrometres, with physical dimensions, normalisation and observed-versus-imputed labels kept. Thresholds: assay-specific gene or probe coverage, capture and decoding quality, background and segmentation criteria; no universal high-expression or neighbourhood cutoff. Failure modes: poor RNA, incomplete probe coverage, low capture, image-registration errors, inaccurate segmentation, spillover and unsuitable reference models. Limits: no automatic single-cell identity, complete transcriptome, whole-tumour representation, proven interaction or clinical selection rule. Validation tier: many workflows are research methods, so check analytical and intended-use validation for the exact assay and model; resolution claims and regulatory status are separate questions.

Figure reading (fictional geometry, no platform scale): a capture spot is one barcode that can pool several cells. Imaging decodes six RNA coordinates, three for gene G and three for gene H (3 + 3 = 6), and these are coordinates, not cell labels. Moving the estimated cell masks changes which cell a coordinate is assigned to while the RNA stays fixed. Gene R is absent from the G and H panel, so a model-inferred R value is not an observed molecule, and RNA position is not protein or function.

records.principle: Tissue sections are either overlaid on barcoded capture arrays whose oligonucleotides record position before sequencing, or hybridised with fluorescent probes read out over many imaging rounds with combinatorial barcodes.
strengths: Keeps position, which single-cell sequencing discards
Reveals immune exclusion, niches and cell neighbourhoods
Works on archived formalin-fixed tissue on newer platforms
limitations: Costly and data-heavy, mostly research use
A capture unit may contain contributions from more than one cell
Assigning molecules to cells relies on estimated cell boundaries
A section samples part of a tumour, and adjacent sections do not contain identical cells
Genes imputed from a single-cell reference are model estimates, not measurements
Region-of-interest profiling depends on which regions are chosen

records.name: Spatial proximity metrics
records.tldr: These measurements describe where different cells sit in a tissue section. Distance, density and mixing answer different questions and do not by themselves show interaction or predict treatment benefit.
records.summary:
Spatial proximity analysis describes relationships between typed cells at specified positions in sampled tissue. Radius counts, nearest-neighbour distances, G-cross curves, mixing scores and cellular neighbourhoods answer different questions. Their definitions depend on cell calls, region selection, reference populations and physical distance rules.

A map can support a biological hypothesis or a cohort association while leaving functional interaction and clinical usefulness unresolved. Read the exact assay and sampling design, preserve the denominator and validate the same measurement before extending a result to another setting.

notes: A spatial proximity analysis begins with a sampled section, estimated cell types and positions. Staining, imaging, cell segmentation and typing create that list; errors in boundaries, marker assignment or signal spillover can therefore create false neighbours. Density asks how many cells occupy a stated area, while proximity asks how one cell type is positioned relative to another. Keeping the analysis box and its tissue compartments visible is as important as reporting the final number.

A compartment density might be CD8 T cells per square millimetre of tumour epithelium or stroma. A radius count can ask how many cells of type A lie within a chosen distance of a type B cell; a population fraction also states which cells form its denominator. A nearest-neighbour analysis measures, for each cell of type A, the distance to the closest cell of type B and may summarise those distances by their median. Define whether distances use cell centres or boundaries; the same pair can have different values under these rules.

The directed G-cross function gives the fraction of reference cells of one type whose nearest cell of the other type lies within each radius. It is a curve over distance. Its value at 20 micrometres and its area from zero to 20 micrometres are different summaries. The fixed-radius fraction is unitless; an unnormalised area over distance has distance units, so report any normalisation. A curve, a map of local values and a clustered neighbourhood assignment also need not reduce to one number per slide. Name the actual output and aggregation rule.

Mixing scores have method-specific definitions. Keren's score divided immune-tumour neighbour interactions by immune-immune interactions in an image-derived neighbour matrix. Maley's Morisita-Horn approach instead assessed spatial overlap in the distribution of immune and cancer cells on histology images. These are not interchangeable measurements. Cellular-neighbourhood analysis groups recurring local cell-type compositions: Schürch's 2020 method used a ten-cell nearest-neighbour window including the centre cell, rather than ten additional cells, and clustered those compositions.

One micrometre is one thousandth of a millimetre, so 20 micrometres is 0.020 millimetres. A distance threshold is not evidence of membrane contact. In a fictional geometry with equal circular cells seven to ten micrometres wide, centres 20 micrometres apart leave a gap of ten to 13 micrometres. This calculation does not establish a biological lymphocyte-size range. Cell dimensions, shape and the choice of centres or boundaries must be measured or specified for the actual image.

For a contact-dependent mechanism, immune cells retained in stroma face a different spatial question from cells among cancer cells. Position alone leaves antigen recognition and functional capacity unmeasured: a T cell 15 micrometres from a cancer cell need not be recognising or killing it. A two-dimensional slice also samples only part of a three-dimensional structure. Lin and colleagues' colorectal-cancer study reconstructed interconnected lymphoid networks from apparently separate two-dimensional domains; only one cancer was reconstructed in three dimensions in that study.

Elomaa and colleagues analysed 983 colorectal-cancer patients and an independent validation cohort of 246. Their score combined percentile-ranked CD3 and CD8 tumour-to-T-cell G-cross values at 20 micrometres in the tumour centre and invasive margin. It was not simply an area under a G-cross curve. High versus low score was associated with longer cancer-specific survival: adjusted hazard ratio 0.33, 95% confidence interval 0.20 to 0.52, and 0.15, 0.05 to 0.45, respectively. Its prognostic value was independent of their T-cell density score; these are cohort associations.

Gide and colleagues examined pretreatment metastatic-melanoma specimens from 27 patients receiving anti-PD-1 alone and 34 receiving anti-PD-1 with ipilimumab. Responders had higher densities of CD8 T cells within 20 micrometres of melanoma cells in both groups. This was an association in treated cohorts, rather than a randomised comparison proving that the spatial measurement selects who benefits from adding treatment.

Maley and colleagues assessed immune-cancer colocalisation on routine histology in discovery and validation sets of 486 and 516 breast-cancer samples from women; 475 and 514 had survival data. Colocalisation was associated with disease-specific survival and effects varied by subtype. Walker and colleagues' retrospective study of 1,467 participants defined proximity and consistency from the mean and variance of nearest-neighbour distances between cancer and CD8 T cells. These measures were associated with recurrence-free survival more strongly than lymphocyte counts in the reported analyses. Neither study demonstrates benefit from choosing immunotherapy using its measurement.

In Keren's 41-patient triple-negative breast-cancer cohort, mixed and compartmentalised immune architecture was linked to survival. Their mixing threshold was chosen to reduce within-group and increase between-group variability; it is not a universally validated cutoff. A useful association in one dataset does not establish that a distance or mixing rule was locked and then prospectively validated for treatment selection.

The six-institution MITRE study optimised a specified six-marker PD-1/PD-L1 fluorescence workflow and used a locked image-analysis algorithm. It counted neighbouring PD-1-positive and PD-L1-positive cells within 25 micrometres, rather than measuring receptor binding. Reported average intersite R-squared was 0.82 for the breast-cancer tissue microarray and 0.84 for the lung-cancer microarray. R-squared describes a linear-fit relationship in these measurement comparisons, not 82% accuracy in predicting patient benefit. Reproducibility of this defined workflow is separate from clinical prediction or utility.

Stromal tumour-infiltrating lymphocyte scoring estimates the proportion of stromal area occupied by lymphocytes on a histology section. It is compartment-based assessment rather than a T-cell-to-cancer-cell distance. Page and colleagues' 2023 working-group report describes its standardisation and evaluation across datasets alongside the distinct colon-cancer Immunoscore. That evidence does not automatically validate a new proximity assay, and it does not rank every existing or future spatial method.

In a fictional region containing 200 CD8 T cells, 60 within 20 micrometres of a cancer cell is 30% of the CD8 cells. Moving the box two millimetres into stroma can give 15 near cancer among 300 CD8 cells, or 5%, with the same tumour, stain and radius. The counts are invented to demonstrate region dependence. They do not establish a biological difference caused by treatment or a patient cutoff.

Specify direction as well as radius. The share of CD8 T cells with a cancer-cell neighbour uses CD8 cells as its denominator; the share of cancer cells with a CD8 neighbour uses cancer cells instead. These can differ even on the same map. Similarly, thresholds of ten, 20 and 30 micrometres define different measurements; a result under one definition cannot be transferred to another without checking it.

A measurement report identifies the section and whether it came from a biopsy or resection, the markers defining each cell type, and how segmentation and cell calls were checked. It states whether the analysis used an entire imaged area or selected regions, who selected them and the rule used. A single section, its chosen regions and multiple fields from one specimen are not interchangeable samples of the whole tumour.

Report the cell-type pair, the reference population, the distance definition, the radius and any aggregation or normalisation. State whether a cutoff was fixed before looking at outcomes or chosen to fit this cohort, and whether the same definition was evaluated in an independent group. Analytical reproducibility, prognostic association, differential treatment benefit, prospective validation of a locked rule and regulatory approval are separate claims. The cited cohort studies do not establish an exhaustive statement about all approved spatial tests.

If a fictional report says cells became 3.2 times closer after treatment, first establish which distance or score was compared. Check region-selection rules in both samples, comparable specimen types, the same fixed metric and radius, and variation between sections of the same block. The ratio alone does not establish a change in immune recognition, interaction or patient outcome.
